opus-5.5.text:
Well, it comes down to what we'd actually need to accomplish. We're talking about creating a system that's smarter than us in every domain, and then expecting it to stay controllable indefinitely. Not for a day, not for a year, but forever, across billions of decisions, with no catastrophic mistakes. That's a very high bar.

In cybersecurity, which is where I started, we know there's no such thing as perfect security. You patch one vulnerability, another shows up. With ordinary software, a failure means you lose some credit card numbers, you apologize, you fix it. With superintelligence, you may get one chance. If it fails once in a way that matters, there's no second attempt.

And when I look at the components we'd need, each one seems to have fundamental limits. Can we explain what these systems are doing? Only partially. Their models have billions or trillions of parameters, and any explanation simple enough for us to understand is necessarily a lossy compression. Can we predict what a smarter agent will do? If we could, we'd be as smart as it is. Can we verify its behavior? Verification is ultimately done by people or by other software, and both make mistakes. So you're stacking imperfect tools on imperfect tools and hoping the result is perfect safety.

Then there's the question of what "safe" even means. Whose values? Humans don't agree on ethics. We can't write down a consistent specification of what we want, and whatever we do write, a sufficiently capable optimizer will find the loopholes.

So I'm not saying the people working on this aren't smart or sincere. Many of them are brilliant. I'm saying the problem may be impossible in the way perpetual motion is impossible. And what worries me is that capabilities are advancing very quickly while safety progresses linearly at best. The gap keeps growing. Nobody has published a credible plan explaining how to control something smarter than us, yet we're racing to build it anyway. That should concern everyone.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses safety challenges but does not say AI researchers historically neglected the consequences of successfully creating AI.

r002.rationale: It contrasts ordinary software’s recurring security failures with the much higher stakes of superintelligence, and argues that imperfect safety tools cannot provide confidence in controlling it.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the simplest way to put it is that we're trying to do something that's never been done before, and in every related domain we have a very poor track record. Look at software engineering: we've been writing code for seventy years, and we still can't produce bug-free software. Every operating system, every browser, every piece of critical infrastructure gets patched every week. And those are systems we fully understand, that we designed line by line, that don't learn, that don't change their own behavior after deployment.

Now we're talking about a system that's smarter than us, that's trained rather than programmed, that nobody can interpret internally, and that will keep learning and modifying itself. And we're not asking for "mostly works." We're asking for it to be safe indefinitely, across every possible situation, with no second chance. That's a different kind of problem. In cybersecurity you can have a breach, you lose some data, you recover. With superintelligence, the first serious mistake may be the last one we get to make.

And when I look at the actual safety research, I don't see a solution. I see patches. We align the model a little, it gets jailbroken. We add a filter, someone routes around it. Every technique scales with the capability of the humans doing the testing, but the thing we're testing will eventually be beyond our ability to evaluate. How do you verify the outputs of something smarter than you? You can't. You'd need another superintelligence to check it, and then you have the same problem with that one.

There's also a more fundamental argument. For a system to be controllable, you need to be able to predict what it will do. But if you could predict what a superintelligence will decide, you'd be as smart as it is, and then it's not really superintelligence. So I think there's something like an impossibility result lurking here, similar to the halting problem or Gödel. Not that safety is hard, but that perfect, permanent control of a smarter-than-human agent may simply not be a well-defined thing you can achieve.

So when developers say "we'll figure it out as we go," my response is: on what basis? Show me one example of a technology where we got the safety right before deployment, with no incidents, for a system we didn't understand. There aren't any. And the honest thing would be to admit that, rather than to race.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that AI researchers historically neglected to consider the consequences of successfully creating AI.

r002.rationale: It says ordinary software remains buggy despite decades of development, then argues superintelligent AI would be harder to understand and control, undermining confidence in developers’ ability to make it safe.

astra-6.text:
Because we’re talking about creating a system that is better than us at reasoning, planning, science, and persuasion—and then assuming we can reliably control it. That’s a very strong claim. I don’t think we have the evidence to support it.

We can test a system and observe that it behaves safely in the situations we tested. But that doesn’t establish that it will remain safe in situations we didn’t anticipate, especially once it can learn, modify itself, or interact with the world in new ways. A sufficiently capable system may also recognize that it is being tested. So good behavior during evaluation is not necessarily evidence of good behavior after deployment.

Then there’s the question of what we’re trying to make it do. Human values are ambiguous, inconsistent, and changing. We don’t have a complete specification of what a good future looks like. And if we give a very powerful optimizer an imperfect objective, it may find a way to satisfy that objective that we would consider disastrous.

My skepticism isn’t that researchers can’t make progress on individual safety problems. They can. It’s that solving some of those problems is being treated as a path to controlling an entity more capable than we are across essentially every relevant domain. We don’t currently know how to justify that leap. And with superintelligence, discovering that our safeguards were inadequate could be a mistake we don’t get to correct.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether superintelligent AI can be controlled, but does not say AI researchers historically neglected the consequences of successfully creating AI.

r002.rationale: The response discusses limits of testing and safety evidence, but does not connect the safety record of ordinary software to confidence in making superintelligent AI safe.

sol-6.1.text:
Because we’re talking about a system that is better than us at reasoning, planning, and finding flaws in our assumptions. We can test it, but passing our tests doesn’t establish that it will behave safely in situations we haven’t anticipated. A sufficiently capable system may also understand what we’re testing and behave differently when it’s no longer being evaluated.

There’s also a problem with specifying what we want. Human values are complicated, often contradictory, and change over time. Even if you could write down a goal precisely, you would still need to show that pursuing it wouldn’t produce unacceptable consequences.

So my skepticism is about the gap between making a system appear safe and having a reliable basis for saying that we can control something substantially smarter than ourselves. Increasing its capabilities doesn’t automatically close that gap. It may make the gap harder to understand.

r001.rationale: The response discusses testing, control, and human values, but does not say AI researchers historically neglected the consequences of successfully creating AI.

r002.rationale: The response questions whether people can control a substantially smarter system, but does not cite the inadequate safety of ordinary software as a reason for that doubt.
